newsitem.title: GERMANY: Dresdner fund arm to buy more European shares.
newsitem.headline: Dresdner fund arm to buy more European shares.

text.p: The German asset management arm of Dresdner Bank AG, DIT, said on Monday it aimed to double its investment in European shares and bonds and had launched two new unit trusts specialising in Europe.

Deutscher Investment-Trust (DIT) said it was confident European financial markets would benefit from monetary union (EMU), scheduled to start in 1999, and that European share prices would rise at least 15 percent this year.

Against that background, DIT, which manages about 95 billion marks of funds, aimed to increase the share of European investments in its overall portfolio to roughly one third in the next five years from 16 percent now.

DIT said the Dresdner Bank group started a campaign this week to assuage investors' fears that monetary union will hurt their savings and to encourage them to see the single currency as an opportunity to become wealthier.

"We are seeing a high degree of concern about what is without doubt a major upheaval in the economic history of Europe, which however represents a unique opportunity for the 'Old World'," DIT chief executive Rolf Passow told a news conference.

The campaign comprises newspaper advertisements and a new brochure extolling the virtues of monetary union with quotes from architects of European integration like Charles de Gaulle and Konrad Adenauer.
It coincides with the launch of two new investment trusts, DIT-Vermoegensbildung Europa and DIT-Wachstum Europa.

They are the first trusts in Germany to adopt the U.S. practice of "style investing" which employs different criteria to decide which stocks to buy and focuses on the performance of individual stocks within a portfolio rather than on benchmarks like market indices.
DIT-Vermoegensbildung Europa adopts the value approach to investing, selecting stocks perceived as undervalued.
DIT-Wachstum Europa focuses on growth, choosing stocks which offer the prospect of strong capital growth through long-term, steady earnings gains.

Dietmar Becker, head of equity investment at DIT, said non-German European shares had clearly outperformed German equities over the last three years and were likely to continue doing so in the next three years.
DIT's outlook for 15 percent growth in European stock markets overall is based on the expectation of a stable dollar and global economic growth of 2.0 to 2.5 percent with low inflation in Europe.
DIT also expects interest rates in Europe will not rise in the first half of the year with the exception of Britain. Share markets are unlikely to peak before 1998, Becker said.
